"Maybe there's a little bit of alcohol that might kill off some of the bacteria, but it's not really doing much to stop you from sweating."

Dr Sebaratnam says whole-body deodorants can contain ingredients that help to absorb moisture, "like silica, arrowroot powder, tapioca or cornstarch".

"The products don't stop you sweating per se, but the liquid is quickly absorbed and so don't have that wet sensation," he says.

Dr Koh Belic says that if you do experience body odour due to sweat, "you might prefer using antiperspirants".

She says antiperspirants work by blocking the output of sweat glands, "so that the sweat doesn't come out" and bacteria can't feed off it.

'Creating a problem where there isn't one'

While he says anything you apply to your skin could provoke an allergic reaction, Dr Sebaratnam believes all body deodorant products are mostly "innocuous".

Chris Callewaert, a microbiologist and sweat researcher based in Europe, says the "new trend" does have the potential to interfere with the skin microbiome.

Chris Callewaert says introducing a new product to certain areas of the skin can create issues. (Supplied: Dr Chris Callewaert)

The skin microbiome is the complex ecosystem of microorganisms including bacteria and fungi that protect against pathogens and maintain overall skin barrier health.

"The more antibacterial ingredients present in a skin cosmetic, the bigger the impact on the skin microbiome," says Dr Callewaert, who also goes by the name "Dr Armpit".

He says using the products "can lead to unwanted side effects, among which are odours, infections, rashes and sensitive skin".

Dr Koh Belic agrees and says the products may create a problem "that doesn't need to exist".

Using them in sensitive areas, like around your genitals, is not recommended.

Marketing 'shame and embarrassment' about bodies

Dr Newton believes cosmetic companies are "creating problems related to the body and health" and then selling solutions, "in this case deodorants".

"We know that sweat is a normal part of life, and body odour tends to occur alongside sweat," she says.

How social ads target women There's a big market online for products to put in or on our genital areas, blurring the lines between hygiene, cosmetics and medicine.

"But certainly, from an advertising and a social perspective, companies promote ideas to increase the shame and the uncertainty related to our bodies and our health."

She says encouraging the use of these deodorants with terms like "pits, privates and beyond" also creates a "vagueness and ambiguity" for consumers.

"It is misleading or encouraging [consumers] to engage in risky behaviours [such as using them on or near genitals] that could harm their bodies and their health."

Our experts say if you're worried about body odour or sweat, you should seek advice from a healthcare professional.

Dr Callewaert says the underlying cause of excess sweat and odour can be multifaceted and may include stress, diet, and hormones.

Dr Sebaratnam says it might also be a sign of a medical condition.

"Don't navigate it alone," he says.

" There are effective medical treatments for excessive sweating that impacts your quality of life. "

This is general information only. For personal advice, you should see a qualified medical practitioner.

World.title: Mother breaks silence as new details emerge in Hayden Panettiere's death
World.content:
Hayden Panettiere's on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were at the South Carolina apartment where the actor died over the weekend, according to a police report.

A Greenville police officer who responded to the residence Sunday afternoon was met by the brothers and observed paramedics performing CPR on an unresponsive woman, the report released Tuesday, local time, said.

"The patient did not seem to have any obvious physical reasons to be unresponsive," the officer noted.

After attempting lifesaving measures, the emergency workers declared Panettiere dead.

In her final months, Hayden Panettiere chose to be 'brutally honest' The actress, who died on Sunday aged 36, spoke openly about the hardships she experienced throughout her decades in the spotlight.

No cause has been determined, and her death remains under investigation.

An autopsy found no signs of trauma, and police said officers saw no signs of foul play.

The one-time child star, who soared to fame in the TV shows Heroes and Nashville while enduring struggles with alcohol addiction and depression, would have turned 37 this week.

The report comes as Panettiere's mother, Lesley Vogel, spoke about the death, saying her daughter found herself on the wrong path.

"I think Hayden sadly lost her way, and I wish it were different," she told NBC.

"I wish she had stayed true to herself because she had many incredible attributes."

Before her death Hayden Panettiere said she was not speaking with her mother, Lesley Vogel. (Getty Images: Frazer Harrison)

In her 2026 memoir, Panettiere described a turbulent relationship with her mother, whom she called a "perfectionist", and alleged that she had superglued a fallen tooth back into Panettiere's mouth so she wouldn't lose a job.

Hickerson had history of abuse

The appearance of Brian Hickerson at the scene of Panettiere's death followed charges of abuse and a fraught relationship.

Hickerson was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner.

He served a short time in jail due to the case.

He was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management and Alcoholics Anonymous sessions.

He completed the terms and recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanours.

A Los Angeles judge denied that request Thursday.

US star Hayden Panettiere dies aged 36 Hayden Panettiere, star of Heroes and Nashville, has died. She was 36.

Panettiere wrote of Hickerson's time behind bars, hoping it would change him.

"I needed him to admit his wrongs and change because of them, but I didn't want to traumatise him in an irreversible way," she wrote.

The police report, which is heavily redacted, said the responding officer first spoke with Zach Hickerson, who said the unresponsive woman was his brother's girlfriend.

"Brian did not become emotional until EMS declared her officially deceased," the officer said.

Also redacted is a list of medications that Panettiere had been taking.

Ex-fiancé vows to share memory with daughter

In her book, Panettiere described lifelong scars from her early fame, and acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter, Kaya, with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014.

Panettiere's daughter, now 11, began living with Klitschko full-time in Ukraine when she was two.

At the time, the actor was struggling with her mental health and addiction.

She entered rehab in 2015 while filming Nashville.

Ex-fiance Wladimir Klitschko said Panettiere remained an "important part of my life". (Instagram)

Klitschko has also broken his silence, saying "nothing will erase the times we shared".

"To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was," he shared on Instagram.

Panettiere had endured numerous family struggles and tragedies.

Her parents' marriage was strained and eventually ended.

Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023 at age 28.

Hollywood has continued to mourn the star's shocking death, with her director in Ice Princess paying tribute to its dual protagonists.

Panettiere starred in the 2005 Disney film alongside Michelle Trachtenberg, who also died in February, aged 39.

"I remember them both with huge affection, how they were 20-odd years ago, at that relatively uncomplicated time of their lives," director Tim Fywell told Variety.

" Two shining talents gone far too soon. "

AP/ABC

World.title: Man charged with murder over alleged stabbing south of Brisbane
World.content:
A 47-year-old man has been charged with murder and a woman is under police guard in hospital after an alleged stabbing south of Brisbane on Tuesday.

Emergency services were called to reports of an altercation between three people at a house on Lubach Street at Beenleigh about 4:45pm.

Police will allege the 66-year-old was stabbed in the altercation.

Officers attempted CPR but the man was declared dead shortly after they arrived.

Emergency services were called to reports of an altercation between three people at a house on Lubach Street at Beenleigh. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The Karalee man has been charged with murder and is due to face Brisbane Magistrates Court today.

A 43-year-old Beenleigh woman is in hospital under police guard and is expected to help police with their investigation.

Police said all three people knew each other.

Queensland Ambulance Service said a man in his 40s with an arm wound and an uninjured woman were both taken to hospital.

World.title: ‘I love opening’: Shocked but excited, Renshaw ready to make Test spot his own
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I love opening’: Shocked but excited, Renshaw ready to make Test spot his own Daniel Brettig August 19, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Matt Renshaw was still in something of a daze as he picked up his bags to resume life as a Test cricketer, a decade after being a “little baby” in the national team. Renshaw was at home in Brisbane with his wife Josie and their two young children on Monday night when the call came from selection chair George Bailey, telling him to get ready to join Australia as they try to overturn a surprise defeat by Bangladesh in Darwin. Matt Renshaw with Pete Handscomb after his first Test hundred in January 2017. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Former 2GB broadcaster’s lawyers continue cross-examination of ‘Complainant C’ in indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day 11 of Alan Jones’ criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleague Perry Duffin will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear further evidence today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones arrives at court on day 11 of his trial. Nine News

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent.

“C”, a former staffer to Jones, faces further cross-examination today by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC.

Bashir asked him yesterday about a series of friendly text messages and other communications he had with Jones after the alleged assaults. He has agreed that some of the messages were suggestive.

The complainant told the court he hated reading the messages. Bashir put to him that he felt this way because they exposed his allegations as fabrications, prompting an angry outburst from “C”.

“No, because I don’t like the references to him talking about my c--- ... I don’t like hearing a bloke, 40 years older, writing to a straight guy, wanting to play with his penis. Get real,” “C” said.

“C” told the court earlier this week that he broke down sobbing when he told then-2GB host Ray Hadley about the alleged assaults.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Bashir said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Melbourne High School principal quits for new role
World.content:
The principal of one of Melbourne’s most prestigious state schools will resign in September for a role with the Education Department after almost six years in the top job. Tony Mordini is known as a visionary at the all-boys school in South Yarra, but his tenure has not been without controversy. Melbourne High principal Tony Mordini is stepping down from the role. Justin McManus. “To have served this remarkable school community has been both professionally rewarding and personally enriching,” Mordini said in an email to the school community. Mordini’s new position will be a principal adviser role for the Department of Education, which he said would allow him to “contribute to public education at a system-wide level.



Related Article High school Melbourne High students to shift into portables after ‘extreme’ safety concerns raised “It will draw upon my experience in school leadership, my work in boys’ education, my service within the judiciary, and my scholarship and research in mental health.” Melbourne High School is a state-funded, academically selective school for boys in years nine to 12, with strong VCE results. The Age last month revealed mounting safety concerns regarding the school’s historic Gothic-style main building. As many as half of Melbourne High’s classes could be held in demountables on the school’s hockey field while the Victorian State Building Authority works on electrical and fire-system remediation works. Determined to clean up the school finances following his appointment, Mordini was instrumental in ending an embezzlement scandal that robbed the school’s coffers of more than $430,000 between 2012 and 2021.



Mordini set about changing a single-tier payment authorisation system that had given the school’s former business manager unchecked access to its bank accounts. The process led to the discovery that Frances Walshe had transferred funds from the school bank account into her own account more than 250 times to feed a gambling habit. Walshe resigned on the spot and was sentenced to two years in jail, with a minimum of 14 months, in 2023. The school’s most recent annual report recorded $3,252,076 in total funds at the end of 2025. Staff satisfaction was reported at 45 per cent in the same report, almost 15 per cent below the state average. Consultants were called in at a cost of about $80,000 to work with staff to identify the issues.



In term two 2024, Melbourne High completed a review to inform the development of the next four years. Staff members reported feeling that the leadership structure needed to be revised to ensure it was “cohesive, visible, positive and focused on building relationships between staff and leadership members”. “On the SSS [School Staff Survey], the percentage endorsement for Instructional leadership was 13 per cent, which was 47 per cent below the result of similar schools,” the report said. Mordini is currently an Honorary Fellow at the Melbourne Graduate School of Education at the University of Melbourne, and has formerly worked as an assistant principal at Mount Ridley College – one of the state’s largest metropolitan public schools. “Thank you for the privilege of serving as your principal,” Mordini said.

World.title: Jaws made us scared to enter the water. This play reveals the real horror
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Steven Spielberg was only 27 when he directed Jaws, but the film redefined the creature feature the same way his E.T. later made aliens cuddly and Jurassic Park rekindled our love of dinosaurs. Those movies dazzled viewers by pushing the limits of technology, but Jaws was most notable for what it didn’t show. The shark at its centre was a mess. The 1200-kilogram leviathan’s mechanical malfunctions were notorious. Spielberg insisted on filming in open water, and the behemoth’s behaviour in the brine was so poor that the director had to invent a slew of film techniques covering up for the absence. Those menacing point-of-view shots of swimmers’ legs? The victims yanked beneath the waves by an invisible terror? The two notes signalling the shark’s approach? They’re why the film is so chilling, despite how rarely we glimpse the misbehaving animatronic monstrosity the crew affectionately dubbed Bruce. Cinematographer Bill Butler, standing, and director Steven Spielberg with “Bruce” during the filming of Jaws. Peacock/Universal Pictures via AP The Shark is Broken is a play that dramatises the production’s off-screen challenges, as experienced by the fractious, larger-than-life personalities of its three leads. There’s Richard Dreyfuss, the New Hollywood young buck desperate to prove his chops. Roy Scheider is the perma-tanned hot-shot fresh off Oscar-bait such as Klute and The French Connection. And then there’s the legendary Robert Shaw, the British actor who’d played everything from Bond villain to Henry VIII. The larger-than-life stars of Jaws, from left, Robert Shaw, Roy Scheider and Richard Dreyfuss. AP The shark in Jaws is what literary types call a structuring absence: you don’t see much of the big fish, but its presence looms large. The structuring absence of The Shark is Broken might well be Robert Shaw himself. The play is the brainchild of his son, actor and writer Ian Shaw. Writing a play about his father – and sometimes playing the role – meant grappling with the man who died of a heart attack when his son was only eight.



For most of his career, Ian avoided mention of his famous father. Nepo babies in showbiz are nothing new – even Aeschylus and Euripides had kids who followed in their footsteps – but the younger Shaw had built his career on his own terms long before The Shark is Broken was a glimmer in his eye. “Bruce” gets the better of Robert Shaw’s Quint in Jaws. Getty That seed was planted after he met Richard Dreyfuss in Birmingham. The veteran actor was directing a production of Hamlet when Ian introduced himself as the son of his Jaws co-star. The meeting didn’t go well. “He looked like he’d seen the ghost of Hamlet’s father and sort of crumpled and sat down. I thought: ‘Well, I’ve blown this.’” Related Article Stage You probably never wonder who’s packing your parcels. Perhaps you will now The younger Shaw had forgotten the lessons he had absorbed from Carl Gottlieb’s famous book The Jaws Log, which describes a volatile off-screen relationship between Dreyfuss and Ian’s father during filming. The rivalry among the Jaws cast was long a sore point for Dreyfuss, who claims that reports of his bratty behaviour are overblown. He and the playwright met again at the US premiere of The Shark is Broken. Richard Dreyfuss and Ian Shaw “summoning his father” at the Broadway premiere of The Shark is Broken. Bruce Glikas/WireImage Ian Shaw recalled: “I’d loved the film so much and watched it so many times, and the chemistry was so good that I sort of assumed that they were basically friends. It became clear that there was something quite deep going on for Richard and so I walked away, and that gave fuel to the thoughts in my head that there was a very interesting backstory here.”



He quickly shelved the idea, though. “I thought it would be in poor taste, actually… I loved my father dearly and didn’t want to do him a disservice. I thought it was potentially going to be a car crash and terribly embarrassing and my family would be upset.” Loading There was plenty of family to take offence: Robert Shaw had 10 children from three marriages. But after friends convinced him that it was at least worth plumbing the depths of Hollywood’s first legitimate blockbuster, he and co-writer Joseph Nixon knuckled down. When the first draft was complete, they knew they had something on the hook. Robert Shaw, left in Jaws, and his son, Ian, whose play The Shark is Broken, tells the behind-the-scenes story of the making of the film. “But I thought we had something that would be popular on a small scale. We were going to tour it around the UK, taking it to 80-seat venues, putting it in the back of a van.” They arrived at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival with a production as scrappy as the fishing trawler in which the action plays out. The actor performing as Roy Scheider was also the show’s designer, and the three cast members would build the set themselves in the scant minutes before the show began. They’d brought another play by Damon Runyon to the festival to perform on alternate nights. It wasn’t long before the Runyon play was thrown overboard. “Word of mouth got out that [The Shark is Broken] was a good show. People wanted to see this and they couldn’t get tickets. We were sold out and lots of wonderful producers were coming to see it. I was slightly dumbfounded because the Edinburgh Festival is a tricky place. Normally you’re struggling, you’re dragging people off the streets to come and see your show.”



The message was clear: you’re gonna need a bigger theatre. Soon enough the play was booked for a lengthy West End run. A Broadway season followed. From left, Demetri Goritas, Liam Murray Scott and Ian Shaw during the London season of “The Shark Is Broken” in 2021. Getty Images Critics have praised the play’s humour. “We were very conscious of the source material. Jaws is a very funny film. The headline is that it’s a horror film or a thriller. But it’s very funny, and funnier as the years go by,” says Shaw. Related Article The Verdict From Swan Lake to Sugar Plum Scary: enough with the ballerina assassins But Jaws is also a film that takes frequent handbrake turns. One moment you’re in a monster movie, the next a satire of small towns and small minds, and then a rollicking caper on the high seas. “What I love about the movie is the way that you don’t quite know what’s going to happen next,” says Shaw. “It feels like it shifts tone very sharply, and so we wanted to emulate that in the play.” Getting into the heads of its three characters meant devouring every documentary and interview that Shaw and Nixon could find. “Some of [the dialogue] is what they actually said. And then you fill in the blanks. You try to guess what they might have said from how they felt.”

Mordini set about changing a single-tier payment authorisation system that had given the school’s former business manager unchecked access to its bank accounts. The process led to the discovery that Frances Walshe had transferred funds from the school bank account into her own account more than 250 times to feed a gambling habit. Walshe resigned on the spot and was sentenced to two years in jail, with a minimum of 14 months, in 2023. The school’s most recent annual report recorded $3,252,076 in total funds at the end of 2025. Staff satisfaction was reported at 45 per cent in the same report, almost 15 per cent below the state average. Consultants were called in at a cost of about $80,000 to work with staff to identify the issues.



In term two 2024, Melbourne High completed a review to inform the development of the next four years. Staff members reported feeling that the leadership structure needed to be revised to ensure it was “cohesive, visible, positive and focused on building relationships between staff and leadership members”. “On the SSS [School Staff Survey], the percentage endorsement for Instructional leadership was 13 per cent, which was 47 per cent below the result of similar schools,” the report said. Mordini is currently an Honorary Fellow at the Melbourne Graduate School of Education at the University of Melbourne, and has formerly worked as an assistant principal at Mount Ridley College – one of the state’s largest metropolitan public schools. “Thank you for the privilege of serving as your principal,” Mordini said.
