World.title: Jaws made us scared to enter the water. This play reveals the real horror
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Steven Spielberg was only 27 when he directed Jaws, but the film redefined the creature feature the same way his E.T. later made aliens cuddly and Jurassic Park rekindled our love of dinosaurs. Those movies dazzled viewers by pushing the limits of technology, but Jaws was most notable for what it didn’t show. The shark at its centre was a mess. The 1200-kilogram leviathan’s mechanical malfunctions were notorious. Spielberg insisted on filming in open water, and the behemoth’s behaviour in the brine was so poor that the director had to invent a slew of film techniques covering up for the absence. Those menacing point-of-view shots of swimmers’ legs? The victims yanked beneath the waves by an invisible terror? The two notes signalling the shark’s approach? They’re why the film is so chilling, despite how rarely we glimpse the misbehaving animatronic monstrosity the crew affectionately dubbed Bruce. Cinematographer Bill Butler, standing, and director Steven Spielberg with “Bruce” during the filming of Jaws. Peacock/Universal Pictures via AP The Shark is Broken is a play that dramatises the production’s off-screen challenges, as experienced by the fractious, larger-than-life personalities of its three leads. There’s Richard Dreyfuss, the New Hollywood young buck desperate to prove his chops. Roy Scheider is the perma-tanned hot-shot fresh off Oscar-bait such as Klute and The French Connection. And then there’s the legendary Robert Shaw, the British actor who’d played everything from Bond villain to Henry VIII. The larger-than-life stars of Jaws, from left, Robert Shaw, Roy Scheider and Richard Dreyfuss. AP The shark in Jaws is what literary types call a structuring absence: you don’t see much of the big fish, but its presence looms large. The structuring absence of The Shark is Broken might well be Robert Shaw himself. The play is the brainchild of his son, actor and writer Ian Shaw. Writing a play about his father – and sometimes playing the role – meant grappling with the man who died of a heart attack when his son was only eight.



For most of his career, Ian avoided mention of his famous father. Nepo babies in showbiz are nothing new – even Aeschylus and Euripides had kids who followed in their footsteps – but the younger Shaw had built his career on his own terms long before The Shark is Broken was a glimmer in his eye. “Bruce” gets the better of Robert Shaw’s Quint in Jaws. Getty That seed was planted after he met Richard Dreyfuss in Birmingham. The veteran actor was directing a production of Hamlet when Ian introduced himself as the son of his Jaws co-star. The meeting didn’t go well. “He looked like he’d seen the ghost of Hamlet’s father and sort of crumpled and sat down. I thought: ‘Well, I’ve blown this.’” Related Article Stage You probably never wonder who’s packing your parcels. Perhaps you will now The younger Shaw had forgotten the lessons he had absorbed from Carl Gottlieb’s famous book The Jaws Log, which describes a volatile off-screen relationship between Dreyfuss and Ian’s father during filming. The rivalry among the Jaws cast was long a sore point for Dreyfuss, who claims that reports of his bratty behaviour are overblown. He and the playwright met again at the US premiere of The Shark is Broken. Richard Dreyfuss and Ian Shaw “summoning his father” at the Broadway premiere of The Shark is Broken. Bruce Glikas/WireImage Ian Shaw recalled: “I’d loved the film so much and watched it so many times, and the chemistry was so good that I sort of assumed that they were basically friends. It became clear that there was something quite deep going on for Richard and so I walked away, and that gave fuel to the thoughts in my head that there was a very interesting backstory here.”



He quickly shelved the idea, though. “I thought it would be in poor taste, actually… I loved my father dearly and didn’t want to do him a disservice. I thought it was potentially going to be a car crash and terribly embarrassing and my family would be upset.” Loading There was plenty of family to take offence: Robert Shaw had 10 children from three marriages. But after friends convinced him that it was at least worth plumbing the depths of Hollywood’s first legitimate blockbuster, he and co-writer Joseph Nixon knuckled down. When the first draft was complete, they knew they had something on the hook. Robert Shaw, left in Jaws, and his son, Ian, whose play The Shark is Broken, tells the behind-the-scenes story of the making of the film. “But I thought we had something that would be popular on a small scale. We were going to tour it around the UK, taking it to 80-seat venues, putting it in the back of a van.” They arrived at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival with a production as scrappy as the fishing trawler in which the action plays out. The actor performing as Roy Scheider was also the show’s designer, and the three cast members would build the set themselves in the scant minutes before the show began. They’d brought another play by Damon Runyon to the festival to perform on alternate nights. It wasn’t long before the Runyon play was thrown overboard. “Word of mouth got out that [The Shark is Broken] was a good show. People wanted to see this and they couldn’t get tickets. We were sold out and lots of wonderful producers were coming to see it. I was slightly dumbfounded because the Edinburgh Festival is a tricky place. Normally you’re struggling, you’re dragging people off the streets to come and see your show.”



The message was clear: you’re gonna need a bigger theatre. Soon enough the play was booked for a lengthy West End run. A Broadway season followed. From left, Demetri Goritas, Liam Murray Scott and Ian Shaw during the London season of “The Shark Is Broken” in 2021. Getty Images Critics have praised the play’s humour. “We were very conscious of the source material. Jaws is a very funny film. The headline is that it’s a horror film or a thriller. But it’s very funny, and funnier as the years go by,” says Shaw. Related Article The Verdict From Swan Lake to Sugar Plum Scary: enough with the ballerina assassins But Jaws is also a film that takes frequent handbrake turns. One moment you’re in a monster movie, the next a satire of small towns and small minds, and then a rollicking caper on the high seas. “What I love about the movie is the way that you don’t quite know what’s going to happen next,” says Shaw. “It feels like it shifts tone very sharply, and so we wanted to emulate that in the play.” Getting into the heads of its three characters meant devouring every documentary and interview that Shaw and Nixon could find. “Some of [the dialogue] is what they actually said. And then you fill in the blanks. You try to guess what they might have said from how they felt.”

World.title: Reviewer appointed to probe second Immigration IT project
World.content:
The Public Service Commission has appointed a reviewer into another Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment IT project, this time to look at its programme to modernise Immigration New Zealand's systems and services.

The Our Future Services (OFS) programme is [ https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/657277/eyes-turn-to-immigration-s-new-it-project-after-it-misses-first-milestone

a $336 million, seven-year plan] to make visa processing more efficient, mitigate the risks of technology and service failures, provide proactive and sophisticated risk management, and improve customer and user experience.

Following the launch of a review into the Biometric Capability Update project, including whether officials misled ministers, Immigration Minister Erica Stanford asked the commission to look at the broader OFS programme.

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche said the assurance review would provide confidence on cost, governance, management, reporting, and delivery of expected benefits.

"It is important that significant public sector programmes are subject to appropriate scrutiny and assurance. This review will help provide that assurance," he said.

World.title: Fiji PM Rabuka to appeal COI ruling, says he'll resign if appeals fail
World.content:
Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says he will appeal against a High Court decision quashing the report of a Commission of Inquiry (COI) into the appointment of a former head of the country's anti-corruption agency.

The months-long inquiry, which cost the taxpayer around FJ$2 million (NZ$1.5m), has become a major political issue for Rabuka's coalition government.

The COI, headed by Australian judge Justice David Ashton-Lewis, began on 31 October 2024 and was originally due to conclude on 31 January 2025, but continued until 1 May 2025.

Acting on the inquiry's recommendations, Rabuka advised the country's president that the then-commissioner of the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC), Barbara Malimali, should be sacked.

Malimali strongly challenged her suspension and subsequent sacking and launched a judicial review against Rabuka and President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu.

Fiji's High Court ruled in February that Malimali's dismissal was unlawful, a decision immediately appealed by Rabuka.

Then, in June, the High Court rejected Rabuka's attempt to stall its ruling that Malimali was illegally sacked.

Nearly two years after the inquiry was established, Rabuka faced another legal setback when the High Court ruled last Friday that the inquiry report, in its entirety, was null and void.

The High Court found that the inquiry's work after 31 January 2025 was unlawful because its term had not been validly extended, and the president lacked the power to extend its term.

"[The] commission's work from 1 February 2025, and the COI Report dated 1 May 2025, is ultra vires," the judgement stated.

Ultra vires is a legal term meaning beyond lawful authority.

The ruling comes as political parties prepare for Fiji's next general election, which is due later this year.

Following the court's decision, Rabuka told local media he would appeal the decision and would resign if he failed in the Court of Appeal, or if necessary, the Supreme Court.

"I'm appealing the part that implies my activities and touch on my name [regarding] what I had done," he said.

"I'm not the author of the COI. I made the recommendations and it's up to the Attorney-General when he advised me and Solicitor-General. And my personal side, my legal counsel is doing."

Asked if he would reisgn if the appeal failed, Rabuka replied: "Correct."

World.title: 'Not acceptable': Tens of thousands of over 65s can't afford essentials
World.content:
New report on income poverty in people over 65 Nine To Noon Download MP3 11m

Tens of thousands of New Zealanders over the age of 65 are experiencing material hardship and can't afford basic necessities including healthy food and clothing, a new report has found.

The Older Persons Poverty Monitor report, released on Wednesday by the New Zealand Council of Christian Social Services (NZCCSS), delivered a snapshot of poverty and hardship among the country's older population.

The council said the report was the first of its kind in New Zealand, offering a baseline to measure poverty during later life.

The report showed almost 20 percent of New Zealanders over the age of 65 had put off dental and doctor visits due to cost, 147,000 lived in accommodation they did not own (17.25 percent) and 102,000 were living below 50 percent of mean income after housing costs (12 percent),

About 25,000 of New Zealanders in this age bracket were living in material hardship, or living "without the essentials."

The report defined this as having insufficient essentials to "support living, ageing and dying with dignity".

NZCCSS chief executive Alicia Sudden said the report marked a turning point in how New Zealand understands poverty in later life.

"For the first time, we can see and track the scale of poverty among older New Zealanders. What we measure is what we can change - and these first results should make us deeply concerned."

Sudden said the next step was deciding what level of hardship the country was prepared to tolerate.

"We need to draw a line on poverty in later life and decide the minimum standard of dignity every older New Zealander should be able to expect," she said.

"It should not be acceptable that tens of thousands of people reach retirement and still cannot afford healthcare, secure housing or the basic essentials of everyday life."

Women, Māori, and Pacific older people were shown to experience disproportionately higher levels of hardship.

Older Pacific communities had the highest rates of poverty in seven of the nine measures, while Māori were the second most impacted across every

measure.

Presbyterian Support Central chief operating officer Nicola Turner said the findings mirrored what front-line services were seeing across the country.

"We are seeing older people who are not eating properly and certainly cannot afford dental care, glasses, hearing aids or a taxi to a doctor. A lack of money, health status, well-being and independence can be significantly affected in the older population," she said.

"The findings from the [report] reflect what our teams are hearing from older people every day. Now we have the data and evidence that these challenges are widespread and deserve greater attention."

According to the report, many older people were experiencing loneliness, social isolation and age-based discrimination.

The report combined national data with lived experience with consultation with older New Zealanders, community organisations, researchers, service providers and NZCCSS member organisations.

World.title: Documents reveal Health NZ hiring crackdown
World.content:
Health NZ leaders told the Health Minister tight controls on hiring staff were crucial to delivering its budget and that recruitment of any frontline worker was only possible with the sign-off of senior executives.

In a briefing to Simeon Brown last March, then-Health Commissioner Professor Lester Levy and interim chief executive Dr Dale Bramley said strict recruitment rules had been in place throughout 2024/25, and frontline hiring decisions required the sign-off of the regional deputy chief executive.

"This has been coupled with regular close monitoring of recruitment pipelines and the establishment of the HR oversight group," Levy and Bramley wrote. "The expectation is for these controls to remain in place throughout 2025/26."

The documents were released under the Official Information Act to the Public Service Association (PSA), which says Health NZ intentionally delayed recruitment, leaving patients and health workers suffering as a result.

In the same briefing, Levy and Bramley said there would be control over clinical safety, so there were no compromises made to services.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said that was "pure fantasy", saying that roles weren't advertised or filled for months at a time, leading to chemotherapy services being shut down and stroke patients not getting the regular care they deserved.

"These documents expose that the health minister was aware that our health system was not filling hospital vacancies as part of a deliberate savings plan and that patient care has suffered as a result. It's scandalous."

The health minister's office said he told the agency late last year to eliminate bureaucracy in hiring. Health NZ says it no longer uses regional panels for budgeted staff.

'Complex, bureaucratic approval system'

An internal document in June 2024 from then-chief executive Margie Apa showed four regional recruitment forums were set up to approve all hospital and specialist service roles.

An organisation-wide hiring freeze was put in place for all non-frontline roles. This applied to all hospital roles that did not deal directly with patients and all public health jobs that did not deal directly with the community.

The forums included regional directors, medical, nursing, allied health, rural decision-makers, as well as finance and P&C enablers, and were required to regularly sign off hiring decisions.

Fitzsimons said the approval systems were complex and bureaucratic, taking the hiring decisions away from the hospital and service level.

"The approval would take months. In one case, we had a payroll officer, needing to be approved by the chief executive, before the vacancy was advertised.

"Health New Zealand set up a complex, bureaucratic approval system in order to slow down recruitment and save money, and the minister knew about it."

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said recruitment delays severely affected patients. Supplied

The entire Health NZ northern region, which has more than 20,000 employees, was limited to hiring 40 full time roles a fortnight, claimed a union report, called Vacant by Design.

The report quoted workers who described the process as involving "multiple layers of internal and national approvals".

The union said the requirement for regional deputy directors to also sign off frontline staff meant local decisions were made too far away from where the vacancy was.

"The decision about whether to replace an emergency department administrator in Gisborne was made in Hamilton, while the decision about whether to approve a mental health worker in Kaitaia was made in Auckland," the report said.

Six months to fill three neonatal nurse roles

Fitzsimons said the slow recruitment process led to "harrowing examples" of health services being understaffed, with some vacancies not even advertised for months.

"It took six months to replace three neo-natal intensive care nurses in Wellington, a Northland radiologist vacancy sat unapproved for 12 weeks, we saw a regional sonologist vacancy - 28 weeks before it was approved to be filled.

"We are seeing a deliberate strategy, driven by Simeon Brown, where hospital vacancies are not being filled, because they want to save money."

Other examples included an intensive care nurse in the Wellington region not approved after 19 weeks, an emergency department nurse in the southern region not approved for five weeks, a midwife in Counties Manukau not approved after seven weeks and a cardiology service administration clerk not approved 10 weeks later, the report said.

A survey of 1800 PSA members said 76 percent of their team waited more than a month for approval to fill vacancies, and 85 per cent said unfilled roles drove colleagues to stress and burnout.

Fitzsimons said the delayed hiring process led to stroke patients suffering.

Stroke patients should be seen every day, but were commonly only being seen three times a week, impacting their ability to make meaningful progress, the union report said.

In July, Brown announced hospitals could recruit and deploy staff without central sign-off, reducing response times when demand rises, but Fitzsimons said the policy was far from over.

"There is an approval system for new roles in our hospitals that means vacancies are taking too long to be filled and it needs to stop."

Health minister, Health NZ respond

A spokesperson from Brown's office referred to a Letter of Expectations Brown sent to Health NZ in November 2025.

"The minister's position was clear that Health New Zealand 'must continue to remove unnecessary bureaucracy to ensure clinical appointments are delivered in a timely manner, particularly in geographic locations or services experiencing workforce shortages that are directly impacting on patient care'."

A Health NZ spokesperson said it had now changed its hiring processes and the four regional recruitment panels no longer existed.

Current recruitment processes for budgeted roles were now 'two-up', involving the hiring manager's manager, he said.

Management, admin or other roles that weren't budgeted for may need regional review from a forum or committee.

Health NZ introduced a devolved operating model earlier in 2026 to ensure decisions were clinically led and met local need, the spokesperson said.

"While planning and strategy remain a national function, healthcare decisions - including recruitment - are being made closer to care."

The spokesperson said Health NZ did not accept the suggestion recruitment decisions were deliberately leaving services understaffed or that they compromised patient safety.

"Recruitment decisions are made based on service need, workforce availability and patient safety."

World.title: US siblings become NZ refugees as more than 20 Americans claim asylum
World.content:
Government figures show more than 20 Americans have applied for asylum in New Zealand since 2020 - and at least one family was accepted.

Failed US appeals have centred on fears of gun crime, the environment and political climate.

Two American asylum claims of a brother and sister were successfully appealed, because of concerns their dual US/Jordan nationalities would lead them into harm.

Their Jordanian mother had been granted refugee status in New Zealand after she was repeatedly assaulted by her husband while living here, and treated as a servant by his extended family while living in Jordan.

She did not have US citizenship and so could not move there with her 11-year-old son and seven-year-old daughter. She and her husband had divorced, and she had custody of their children.

The tribunal ruled that if the pair were not given refugee status in New Zealand, the US was likely to send them back to Jordan where 'the children would be at risk of breach of their right to be free from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment'.

"In Jordan, they fear being placed in the custody of their father's family and being mistreated by members of their paternal and maternal families," the tribunal said in its decision about the children.

"In the United States, they fear living as unaccompanied minors in institutional or foster care, and that they will be refouled [sent back] to live with family in Jordan."

Their mother had moved to New Zealand with her husband in 2011 when he was a student, saying she suffered intimate partner violence from the start, and was later abused by their families in Jordan.

"The mother was treated by her extended family like a servant and punished for not getting along with her husband. The [children] were treated cruelly by the mother's father, and the father's brothers hit and yelled at the son for any minor wrongdoing. The father's mother also encouraged the son to hit his sister and to censure her."

The family returned to New Zealand, but the violence continued, they were divorced and police were called after she was hospitalised by her injuries. The Family Court made an order barring the father from taking the children overseas.

"The mother also fears that her former husband's family will apply to the United States authorities for the children to return with them to Jordan and they will be exposed to ongoing violence in Jordan at their hands," said the children's 2023 appeal at the immigration and protection tribunal. "She fears, in particular, for her daughter, who will be raised in a climate of violence, and be conditioned to be a subordinate female accustomed to accepting violence."

Among unsuccessful US asylum bids was a woman who wanted protection from Covid-19, gun crime and her own government.

"The tribunal drew the appellant's attention to country information which indicated that while the USA is: politically and socially divided, has high rates of gun ownership, is suffering a rise in belligerent violent anti-government rhetoric, particularly on the far-right such that many people subjectively fear the country is heading towards civil war, the chance that a violent 'civil war' would erupt was remote and speculative."

Despite a significant number of Covid deaths and hospitalisations, "contrary to common parlance, there is in fact no recognised human right to be healthy", and the USA was complying with its obligations.

In another case, an American man claimed he risked persecution for expressing his anti-government views.

"The risk of the appellant being seriously harmed in the United States through environmental degradation, nuclear and toxic waste accidents, or gun-related violence is entirely remote and speculative and well below the 'real chance' threshold," it concluded.

"While the tribunal has no doubt the appellant is sincere in his beliefs and in his desire to live in New Zealand, a country to which he evidently feels a greater affinity than his native United States, the Refugee Convention is not designed to provide a pathway to residence for persons who feel morally and politically disassociated from the direction of their country."

A bisexual Jewish man afraid of returning to the US after president Donald Trump was first elected, also had his appeal dismissed on similar grounds.

A 1995 tribunal finding underpins some of the reasoning: "in the case of an advanced western democracy which generally respects the rule of law, such as the United States, there is a presumption of state protection" of citizens' rights, it said.

A 2008 appeal remarks that the-then Refugee Status Authority "has been unable to establish that there has ever been a successful claim for refugee status made in respect of a person being returned to [the US], either as a national or as a former habitual resident."

Many of the asylum claims cited fear of gun violence, while one man appeared to be fleeing justice.

"He claims that he will be immediately arrested on return to the United States, on the basis of a false criminal record and, owing to his profile, may be held in detention. He claims that he will not be able to seek redress from the US courts and may be repeatedly incarcerated and frustrated by [an unnamed State] District Attorney." He claimed risks to his personal security and freedom from threats made to him as a whistle-blower.

A 68-year-old woman believed Islamist terrorists had killed her relatives in America and had tried to kill her too, but was believed to be suffering from mental health problems. A 42-year-old man said he feared the extent of police violence, as he had been arrested for illegal camping during an Occupy protest, and had been criticised for his political beliefs.

Non-genuine asylum-seekers

Tribunal cases feature some asylum seekers who it decides genuinely fear for their safety or rights but do not meet criteria for asylum - for example, if the chance of someone being persecuted is remote.

However, migrants have also been accused of using the system to instead pursue the work rights that come with an asylum claim.

"While there are genuine claims, there are many claims - the vast majority of claims - that are not meritorious," immigration minister Erica Stanford said in March, as she pointed to high rejection rates of asylum claims.

"And in some instances, people lodge an asylum claim in the final days of another visa, not because they face persecution in their home country, but simply because they want to remain in New Zealand on that visa that everybody wants, the open work visa."

The Age in Australia reported on Sunday that 230 UK citizens in the last year had claimed asylum, with suggestions they were part of a trend of visa overstayers finding a legal loophole to stay and work in Australia.

In New Zealand, refugee claims are still dominated by people from India (683 last year) and China (336). Alongside the US, unusual source countries in the past three years include six Irish asylum seekers and five Japanese.

World.title: NZX appoints Hishaam Mirza as new chief executive
World.content:
The capital markets operator NZX has appointed financial services executive Hishaam Mirza to lead the company.

The NZX has been without a chief executive since May, when Mark Peterson stepped out of the role after many years of service.

NZX chair John McMahon said Mirza was a standout candidate, following a global search to lead the business, which had been struggling to grow the number of listed companies over the past decade.

"Hishaam is a proven strategic leader and recently finished a 14-year tenure at NZ Super, culminating in heading direct investments and managing a team of high-performing investment professionals," McMahon said.

"The Board is delighted with Hishaam's appointment, and we look forward to working with him in delivering NZX's growth strategy to elevate the performance of NZX and New Zealand's capital markets."

Mirza said he was up for the challenge.

"NZX is a highly trusted and well-run market at the heart of New Zealand's economy. The opportunity now is to build greater scale, liquidity and global relevance," Mirza said.

"As chief executive, I'm looking forward to ensuring the exchange - and the Smart and NZX Wealth Technologies businesses - remain strong partners for businesses, investors and government; helping New Zealand businesses grow, innovate and compete internationally, while supporting more New Zealanders to build long-term wealth."

Graham Law will continue to act as chief executive until 14 September, when Mirza takes over.

World.title: Auckland man accused of murdering parents and attempting to murder brother named
World.content:
A 41-year-old man accused of murdering two people and attempting to murder a third on Auckland's North Shore can now be named as Marc Govinden.

The dead victims were his parents, while his brother was injured.

Police found Govinden's brother, Andrew, injured in Birkdale on 28 July.

Govinden was arrested at the scene, and police conducted a welfare check on his parents Raman and Rooksana, who were soon found dead at their Glenfield home.

Justice Mathew Downs set out the charges.

"You are charged with murdering your parents and then attempting to murder your brother," he told Govinden, who appeared in person at Auckland's High Court.

"You will be tried in this court from 2 August next year, I'm setting aside three weeks for your trial."

Justice Downs ordered reports on Govinden's health.

World.title: 'Optics' and 'unfunded promises' - Willis and Sepuloni debate tax
World.content:
Weekly Political Panel: Nicola Willis and Carmel Sepuloni Morning Report Download MP3 15m

Labour's deputy leader says parties need to be careful about optics as they head closer to the election, admitting the continued presence of a member's bill calling for a streaming levy was an oversight.

On Monday, Labour leader Chris Hipkins ruled out a levy on streaming services, only for National to point out Labour had a member's bill in the ballot which would do just that.

The bill was then withdrawn. Labour has blamed an "administrative oversight" for the mixed messaging over the tax, and has confirmed it will not campaign on one.

Labour's deputy Carmel Sepuloni told Morning Report that member's bills were not necessarily part of an election campaign offering.

"As you get closer to the election you do need to be careful about the optics of what you're promoting. Clearly, that bill was still in there and it was an oversight, and it's been taken out now, because we don't want the confusion to be that this is part of Labour's policy offering," she said.

The government had been looking at a streaming levy as well, but decided not to pursue it.

Appearing alongside Sepuloni, National's deputy leader and finance minister Nicola Willis said National ruled it out because "the last thing New Zealanders need is higher charges for their weekly costs."

Sepuloni said National was trying to divert attention from its own "internal ructions."

Willis has frequently been attempting to tie tax proposals from the Greens and Opportunity to Labour, saying Labour has a "hidden bill" it cannot fund.

"Because they have all of these unfunded promises, they're going to be scrambling around looking for cash. And Chlöe Swarbrick has already designed a host of options for them: an inheritance tax, an asset tax, a gift tax, an increase to the corporate tax, an increase to the top personal tax rate."

None of these are Labour policies, with Sepuloni maintaining Labour's only tax will be a capital gains tax (CGT), which Labour says will only affect one in 10 people.

"Labour has one simple tax policy, and the disinformation that is coming from Nicola Willis and National only serves as a deflection for them, so that they don't have to talk about their own track record."

Willis said it was "ludicrous" for Labour to think a CGT would not be worn by more people, with landlords likely to pass costs onto tenants.

World.title: Dees star's ban upheld as AFL tribunal rejects biomechanist evidence bid
World.content:
Melbourne has suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension.

The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen's three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced.

It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons' final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games.

The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at the Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact.

After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.

Melbourne had argued van Rooyen's attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case.

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen.

Aliir Aliir was left concussed after being struck in the head by van Rooyen's swinging arm. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

"The swing of van Rooyen's left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with," Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless.

"Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen's evidence to the contrary.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Even if it was van Rooyen's sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.

"Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm."

The tribunal also found the impact was severe and said there was potential for further injury, such as a facial fracture.

Also on Tuesday night, Brisbane AFLW key forward Dakota Davidson failed to have her one-game striking ban downgraded.

The Lions pleaded guilty and tried to argue the clash with Essendon's Maddi Gay was low rather than medium impact, but the AFLW tribunal upheld the grading.

It means one of the league's top forwards will miss the grand final rematch against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

AAP

World.title: Venus Williams receives US Open wildcard at 46, Serena may follow
World.content:
Venus Williams has received a US Open singles wild card and the tournament is keeping one on hold, perhaps in case her sister Serena wants to join her.

Sloane Stephens, the 2017 US Open champion, was one of six other women to receive a wild card, and the US Tennis Association said the final one was still to be announced.

That will almost certainly go to Serena Williams if she decides she wants to return to the tournament at 44.

Venus Williams received a wild card last year, returning to the grand slam event she won twice for the first time since 2023. The 46-year-old has become the oldest entrant in singles at the tournament since Renee Richards played at 47 in 1981, according to the International Tennis Federation.

Serena Williams could make her return to Flushing Meadows via the final wildcard spot. (Getty Images: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport)

She has continued to play some singles matches, and this week joined Serena for their first doubles tournament together since the 2022 US Open. They lost at the Cincinnati Open in a match tiebreaker against Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

The sisters planned to play at Wimbledon but had to withdraw after Serena injured her knee in her singles match. That marked her first time playing singles since the 2022 US Open, and she indicated afterwards that she hoped to keep competing if she was healthy.

Headlining the wild-card recipients on the men's side are 39-year-old Gael Monfils, a past US Open semifinalist who is set to play his final grand slam tournament before retiring, and Australian Alexei Popyrin, who upset Novak Djokovic in 2024 on the way to the fourth round.

One spot is also being held among the eight men's wild cards. Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 champion at Flushing Meadows, who at 41 is playing his final season, could be a candidate for that.

Australia's Alexei Popyrin has received one of the wildcards in the men's draw. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/David Kirouac)

Also receiving women's wild cards were Carol Young Suh Lee, Reese Brantmeier, Thea Frodin, Leolia Jeanjean and Taylah Preston.

The other men receiving wild cards were two-time reigning NCAA singles champion Michael Zheng, Martin Damm, JJ Wolf, Sebastian Gorzny and Jack Kennedy.

Kei Nishikori, the 2014 US Open runner-up who also is retiring, was given a wild card into the men's qualifying tournament, along with Jordan Lee, Trevor Svajda, Andre Ilagan, Spencer Johnson, Michael Antonius, Andrew Johnson and Daniel Milavsky.

Women given spots in the qualifying tournament were Caroline Dolehide, Janae Preston, Katrina Scott, Ayana Akli, Annika Penickova, Julieta Pareja, Kristina Penickova and Savannah Broadus.

The main draw begins on August 30, with the qualifying tournaments being played earlier that week.

AP

World.title: Darts club membership booms as miners create 'great little community'
World.content:
While darts is typically known as a pub game, to some, it is so much more.

"You don't have to be the best; you just come in, have a beer, listen to music, throw some darts."

Owen Thompson is the Moranbah Darts Club secretary.

The club gets together during the week for a social throw and also host regular competitions and events to raise money for local charities. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

On a wintry Tuesday night, the darts hall in the regional mining town in central Queensland is filling up.

Mates greet each other with a handshake and a slap on the back as the sound of beer cans opening rings through the air.

"I'm no good at it. I just come here every Tuesday to throw stuff at the board and have a few beers," Mr Thompson said.

Loading...

In the town, about 200 kilometres south-west of Mackay, the previous club closed down a few years ago, but the dedication and perseverance of a few members has brought it back to life.

The club now hosts weekly social nights, regular tournaments and charity fundraising events.

"We gradually grew from no-one … to 60 members last season," Mr Thompson said.

Mining country

Moranbah is the largest town in the Isaac region, surrounded by dozens of coal mines. (ABC News: Peter Mullins)

Moranbah is the heartland of coal country in the Bowen Basin.

While the town's official population is 9,425 people (2021 Census), it has a transient workforce that flies, drives or buses in and out of the 47 mines across the Bowen Basin, 30 of which are in the Isaac region.

With long shift-work hours, playing darts has become a source of solace.

"For me personally, I was not doing real well mentally. I found the boys. We come together, clear your head, gives you something to do, gives you a bit of worth," Mr Thompson said.

Fellow club member and vice-president Quinton "Quinno" McCormick constantly tries to recruit his mining mates to have a throw and get out of the mine "camp life".

"We really push the mental health side of things for the people who are away [from] their families … it's just a little somewhere they can escape and live a normal life for a little bit," he said.

It is for anyone who wants to have a go.

Taz and Cassandra Whiteley at the Moranbah darts hall. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Moranbah newcomer Cassandra Whiteley says it is "something different", and its appeal to various fitness levels is a bonus.

"It doesn't have to be high intensity," she said.

"Something different … I enjoy it; it can be as competitive or as fun as you want it to be."

Ms Whiteley, who moved to the town in early 2025, is one of the few female players at the club.

"When we first moved over here, we didn't know a lot of people. I was away at work on training, and my husband actually found the darts place and came down here," she said.

It took three months before she picked up a dart.

"They're a really great group of guys and everyone's lovely, and it's good to get out of the house and have people to talk to and people that genuinely care.

"They're a really great little community here."

Taz Whiteley has competed in darts competitions across Queensland. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Husband Wade Whiteley, known locally as "Taz", a nod to his Tasmanian roots, played competitively in his younger years.

He passes on his tips and tricks to the newcomers.

"Keep your body still, throw with your arm, not your whole body," he said.

"Teaching them rhythm, how to count, a lot of it's counting. Ninety per cent of the game is math, knowing where to go next and not having to stop."

For those keen to take it a bit further than the pub, the World Darts Federation hold its international championship annually.

While darts is not currently featured in the Olympic or Commonwealth Games, Darts Australia has been lobbying to have it included in the latter.

The club uses electronic technology that automatically sends scores to a tablet on the wall. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Back in Moranbah, it is just about bullseyes and banter.

"I don't think I will be, no, [entering the Commonwealth Games]," Mr Thompson said.

"There's a couple that probably think they can; we'll see if they can prove it."

World.title: Ex-AFL player Ricky Henderson sues Fox Sports, AFL over genitals exposure
World.content:
A former professional footballer is suing the AFL and Fox Sports for more than $1.2 million over an incident in which "compromising footage" of him was aired on live television in 2013.

Ricky John Henderson, 37, was an Adelaide Football Club (AFC) player at the time of the incident, on April 6, 2013, in that season's second round.

In court documents seen by the ABC, it is alleged that Mr Henderson was recorded in the changing rooms of the Gabba at half-time as he "stepped away from the player group to adjust his shorts and undergarment, which involved pulling down his shorts and athletic support garment and exposing his genitals".

The lawsuit has been lodged in South Australia's District Court, with Mr Henderson claiming $1,213,867 in damages on the basis the incident was a breach of confidence, an invasion of privacy, and negligent.

In a statement of claim filed with the court, Mr Henderson alleges the "unauthorised use of the footage by way of the broadcast" caused "extreme embarrassment and hurt" as well as "a diagnosable mental illness".

The documents also alleged the broadcast "invaded the privacy and violated the human dignity" of Mr Henderson.

Ricky Henderson was adjusting his shorts when his genitals were exposed on live television. (Fox Sports)

The documents further stated that Mr Henderson had subsequently developed an "acute stress disorder, which developed into a chronic post-traumatic stress disorder".

In addition, the documents also alleged Mr Henderson had experienced low mood and anxiety, feelings of anger and resentment, socially avoidant behaviours, hyper-vigilance, disturbed sleep, loss of motivation, relationship difficulties, and nightmares and intrusive thoughts about the incident.

They also stated the "injuries and resulting disabilities" had led to "periods of total and partial incapacity" for employment and "economic loss and a loss of earning capacity".

In its statement of defence, Fox Sports claimed the footage was not captured in the changing rooms at the Gabba and "denies that the applicant [Mr Henderson] is entitled to the relief claimed or any relief at all".

"Rather, the footage was captured in the 'kicking room' which is a public warm-up area attended by players, coaches, trainers, medical staff and members of the public, including media," the defence statement said.

It said the kicking room was "entirely separate and distinct from the private change-room facilities" where no broadcast cameras were allowed.

Ricky Henderson's genitals were aired during the half time break of the 2013 clash with Brisbane at the Gabba. (Fox Sports)

The defence documents said fixed cameras had been present in the "public warm up area for both home and away teams at all AFL grounds" for several years, and that Mr Henderson was playing his 44th game at the time, including at least two prior matches at the Gabba.

"Mr Henderson knew, or ought reasonably to have known, that the fixed camera captured the footage from the kicking room before, during [including during breaks] and after each match for broadcast," the documents said.

Fox Sports further said it did not broadcast the footage, but had operated the camera in the kicking room and "selected in real-time which camera angles, replays or other vision would be included in the feed delivered to Foxtel for live broadcast".

The documents said Fox Sports "admits" Mr Henderson's genitals were exposed, but "denies" that he stepped away from the group to adjust his shorts and undergarment.

"Fox Sports says that Mr Henderson adjusted his shorts and undergarment near the middle of the kicking room, in the full and open view of other AFC players and staff," the documents stated.

"Fox Sports says that Mr Henderson adjusted his shorts and undergarment directly in front of and in view of the fixed camera.

"All players were on notice of the presence of the fixed camera in the kicking room."

Further, Fox Sports denied the broadcast had caused Mr Henderson, who later went on to play for Hawthorn, extreme embarrassment and hurt or to acquire and suffer any diagnosable mental illness.

In its defence, the AFL said the player ought to have been aware of the fixed camera. (AAP: Mal Fairclough)

In its statement of defence, the AFL also denied that Mr Henderson was entitled to any damages "as alleged, or at all".

The documents similarly stated that Mr Henderson "ought to have known" about the presence of the fixed camera in the kicking room.

"The applicant knew or ought to have known that live footage was streamed from the fixed camera and/or other cameras located in the kicking room," the AFL said.

"The kicking room was not a changing room, and this was known by the applicant or in the alternative ought to have been known by a reasonable person in the position of the applicant."

The AFL also denied breaching any duty of care and denied that Mr Henderson had suffered any injury, disability, or economic loss due to the incident.

However, both Fox Sports and the AFL acknowledged the incident had received significant media, social media and internet attention and was the subject of widespread commentary at the time.

The matter returns to court later this month.

World.title: New mum returns to international 'murderball' with blunt new perspective
World.content:
For Ella Sabljak, the 2026 Wheelchair Rugby World Championships will be a little different to her tournament debut in Denmark four years earlier.

Sabljak, one of four women on the Australian Steelers' mixed-gender roster for the event, is making her return to international competition less than a year after giving birth to her first child.

Along for the ride is baby Billie, slotting into a non-playing but important morale-based role with the team, which has just begun its title defence in the Brazilian city of São Paulo.

Sabljak has returned to international competition accompanied by daughter Billie. (Supplied: Wheelchair Rugby Australia, Albin John)

And motherhood has given Sabljak a blunt new perspective.

"Back then [at the 2022 World Championships] you got to mess around a bit and have fun, where now I want to get in, I want to work hard, and I want to get out," Sabljak told ABC Sport after arriving in camp.

"I'm not into all the mess around like I used to be. If something's going to take up my time away from Billie, it's going to be worth it. She is my number one priority.

"Let's get in, let's f*** s*** up, and let's get out of here."

The road back to international competition

It has not been a straightforward journey back to the international arena for Sabljak, who says she would never have anticipated such a quick return to representative duties.

Only a visit from some of her Steelers teammates in the weeks after giving birth convinced her to return to the sport.

"I was at the stage of postpartum where I didn't know if I wanted to [come back] and they just planted the seed around returning to sport," Sabljak said.

Sabljak was a bronze medallist with the Steelers at the 2024 Paralympics. (Getty Images: Alex Davidson)

But working off a tailored, week-by-week plan, Sabljak plotted her return to elite international competition, all while breastfeeding and working her day job.

Her involvement at the 2026 tournament comes 11 months after Billie's birth, and it is a feat Sabljak never would have thought possible in the immediate aftermath of becoming a mother.

"Not a chance [did I expect to be at the tournament]," she said.

"I thought about it and then we just kind of joked about it, and I was like, 'That's not going to happen! We've got a baby. We've got a small human we need to care for!'"

Bond (left) and Sabljak (right) will line-up for the Steelers at this week's Wheelchair Rugby World Championships in Brazil. (Supplied: Wheelchair Rugby Australia, Albin John)

But Sabljak has felt right at home bringing Billie into the Steelers' camp, with several of her teammates already parents themselves.

Captain Chris Bond, a 15-year veteran of the team with kids aged four and six, told ABC Sport Billie's presence in the camp has been "refreshing" for the whole team.

"We're not their parent, but we get to hang out with them and fulfil that part of us when we're away from our own kids," Bond said.

"It brings out the human side of our team. We are athletes, and we're going to do a job.

"But at the end of the day we're people, and we're humans, and we've got lives outside of sport, and the closer we can connect as people and friends and humans, the better connection we have on court as athletes."

Transitioning to a full-throttle, mixed-gender sport

Wheelchair rugby is known for its big hits and uncompromising physicality. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling)

Previously known by the rather foreboding moniker "murderball", wheelchair rugby is a full-contact sport, renowned for its big hits and end-to-end action.

It does not resemble either rugby code much, with a circular ball permitted to be thrown in any direction.

And unusually for elite-level international sport, it is contested by mixed-gender teams.

Women have traditionally had little representation at the highest level, but a recent rejigging of classification rules as well as a top-down, institutional emphasis on expanding female pathways within the sport have aimed at changing that.

However, questions remain over the long-term viability of the mixed-gender model, with one study in 2025 finding only 2.2 per cent of wheelchair rugby players internationally to be female.

The Steelers are the exception, having focused on increasing female representation over the past few years.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

There are four women in the squad for the 2026 World Championships, accounting for a third of the team.

Bond says the increase in female representation has coincided with a positive cultural shift for the Steelers, who have been the standard-bearers for international competition in the modern era, winning two World Championship titles and two Paralympic golds since 2012.

He says the "rough and tumble, blokey culture" has transformed and the players now "accept anyone for who they are".

For Sabljak, who was a Paralympian in wheelchair basketball before switching codes in 2022, the transition to a mixed-gender sport had its challenges.

"The locker rooms are vastly different; an all-girls locker room versus a boys-dominant locker room is quite, quite different," Sabljak said.

"Just like the conversations that happen, the music that's being played."

Shae Graham became the first woman to represent the Steelers at a Paralympic Games at Tokyo 2020, and Sabljak said she would not have conceived of joining the team if it were not for Graham's breakthrough.

Graham (right) was a trailblazer for Australian women in wheelchair rugby. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Along with Sabljak and Graham, Emilie Miller is now a mainstay of the Steelers set-up, while Lilliana Prucha is making her World Championships debut in Brazil.

"[Having women in the team] is just the norm now, nobody questions it," Sabljak said.

While the Steelers are defending world champions, they enter this year's tournament with a point to prove, having claimed bronze at the 2024 Paralympics, the last major international meet.

That was the team's second-lowest finish across seven international tournaments since 2012, after placing fourth at Tokyo 2020.

Bond says the international standard has never been higher, with "six or seven" nations now serious contenders to finish atop the podium, but believes this Steelers side is "the strongest he's ever been a part of".

"I'm really excited about this team," Bond said.

"We've got so much more depth than we've ever had, we feel really good, really prepared, and the rest is up to the sporting gods."

World.title: AFL policy is to wait while police investigate. The Swans may not
World.content:
The Sydney Swans' declaration that some players are in "serious breach" of club standards has signalled a tougher approach after days of uncertainty over how the AFL would handle a report of an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel where Swans players were staying.

Four Swans players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are understood to be linked to a Victoria Police investigation regarding an alleged sexual assault at an East Melbourne hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

While few details have been made public beyond the allegation itself, Victorian police are continuing to investigate.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

It is not known what breaches of club conduct the club has found.

On Tuesday evening, the Swans issued a statement saying the club would discuss appropriate sanctions and penalties after it finalised interviews with "all players involved".

"We respect there is an ongoing investigation by Victoria Police and any actions we take are independent of this," the statement said.

"The club believes the players are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards, and it is appropriate to take firm action and highlight that any sanction we impose relates solely to those breaches.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women."

Growing pressure on Swans, AFL

Until last night, the club and the league had said relatively little, prompting experts to question whether the AFL's policy of waiting for a criminal investigation to take place if police are involved is a strong enough position for a league that has publicly condemned violence against women.

Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich addressed the media on Monday. (ABC News)

Some of the limited comments from AFL leaders had also drawn criticism, including Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich's mention of the club's extreme disappointment that its players had "found themselves in this situation".

Former AFL Women's star Kate McCarthy was among those who challenged that framing, noting: "Players don't simply 'find themselves in situations'."

Others, including Our Watch CEO Patty Kinnersly, observed some media commentary had focused on finals season while sidelining the "the alleged sexual assault at the centre of this story".

"In the coverage to date we've seen examples of poor reporting that has centred on on-field consequences ahead of a serious, alleged crime," she said.

Advocates welcome new statements from Swans, AFL

The alleged sexual assault has raised questions about how the AFL deals with alleged incidents like this, or if the league is doing enough to prevent incidents in the first place.

Last night AFL CEO Andrew Dillon offered the league's first substantial statement on the alleged sexual assault, labelling the allegations as "serious" and "deeply concerning".

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport," he said.

" It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course. "

Respect Victoria's CEO Helen Bolton, who had earlier criticised the league for not coming out strongly enough, welcomed the fresh statements from the Swans and the AFL.

"I think it's really encouraging that both the club and the AFL have made some really clear and accountable statements about the alleged conduct," she said.

Respect Victoria CEO Helen Bolton had called for a strong response from the AFL. (ABC News: Steven Schubert)

But she said it was disappointing that those statements took so long.

She also stressed the need for a "parallel process" for the AFL to lead its own response to the allegations while the police process was underway, which she said was no different than any other workplace.

AFL investigations pause when police involved

At a policy level, the AFL's default position is to let a criminal investigation run its course when police are involved.

The league's Respect and Responsibility policy outlines that "an AFL investigation will wait until a police investigation has been concluded".

Dr Catherine Ordway describes the AFL's approach to allegations as reactive, not proactive. (Supplied)

Lawyer and sports integrity expert, UNSW scholar Catherine Ordway, described that policy approach as "reactive".

She said it was not in line with best practice across sporting codes, including internationally.

"The AFL waits for the criminal law process to be finalised before taking action against any players or officials," she said.

Dr Ordway said she thought the players should be stood down while a police or AFL investigation took place.

NRL no-fault stand down rule

Since 2019, the NRL has had a policy that if serious charges are laid against a player, the player is stood down while the process moves through the courts.

"There are some pros and cons of that, but I think in terms of fairness that's the right decision," Dr Ordway said.

" There needs to be some strong messaging about how unacceptable violence is against women. "

Australia's two major football codes have different policies for responding to criminal investigations. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Dr Ordway described it as a more "proactive" approach in line with Major League Baseball in the US and the English Cricket Board.

Our Watch, which has delivered educational programs to AFL clubs on gendered violence, said it would support the league adopting a similar rule to the NRL.

"When we're wanting to focus on creating cultures of safety for women, we would support the no-fault stand down that the NRL has done," said Ms Kinnersly, the CEO.

The NRL players association opposed the no-fault stand down policy when it was introduced.

Sydney Swans scheduled to meet overnight

AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher was asked about the no-fault policy on Tuesday but did not say if any equivalent would be opposed by the players' union.

"What we've got here at the moment is allegations, and so I think part of it is understanding exactly what's happened. We should take the time with it to properly understand," he told Triple M.

The Sydney Swans said its board would meet overnight to determine appropriate penalties.

The ABC has contacted the AFL Players Association and the AFL for comment.

World.title: Sydney Swans say players 'in serious breach' of club standards
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly connected to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

The ABC understands four players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are linked to an investigation into an alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in east Melbourne, where the Swans were staying, in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

Victoria Police is investigating, stating this morning that "the exact circumstances are yet to be established and … no one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time".

The club said it interviewed all the players linked to the incident in Melbourne and concluded "firm action" should be taken relating to the breaching of club standards.

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and Isaac Heeney are understood to be linked to a sexual assault investigation. (ABC News/Getty Images)

"The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount," a statement read.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.

"We also want to acknowledge that the care and welfare of our AFLW athletes and staff is of the utmost importance to us as a club.

"They have been and will continue to be offered the support they require, and we acknowledge the impact these allegations have on our female athletes, staff members and the wider community."

Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon did not appear at Swans HQ with the rest of their team on Tuesday and were interviewed by the club off-site with lawyers present.

The Swans board also met Tuesday night to agree on club-imposed sanctions and penalties.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

"Any further sanctions or decisions regarding the outcome of the police investigation would take place after that process is completed," the statement read.

"During this time, we will provide the appropriate support to the players involved in the incident, along with their partners and families.

"The Sydney Swans hold all players and staff at the club to high standards of behaviour and personal conduct. Representing this club carries significant responsibilities both on and off the field, and we expect those standards to be upheld at all times.

"Our focus remains on cooperating fully with the AFL and authorities, maintaining the integrity of the process, and upholding the high standards expected of everyone who represents this club."

'Deeply concerning' incident: AFL CEO

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the allegations around the Swans were "deeply concerning", stressing that, regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, the incident raised wider concerns around the game.

"The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning," he said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon said the effects on a club's season had no bearing on the seriousness of the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport.

"The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected.

"It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course."

Dillon alluded to discussions around the potential sanctions or distractions for the Swans and the potential impact that may have on the second-placed club heading into the AFL finals.

"Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season," he said ahead of the team's final home-and-away game on Sunday.

"Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us.

"As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

"Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.

"Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light."

World.title: Focus should not be on 'football consequences' for Swans, ex-AFLW star says
World.content:
Former AFL Women's star Kate McCarthy has questioned the tone of some of the media coverage around an ongoing police investigation involving Sydney Swans players.

Four Swans players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are understood to be linked to a Victoria Police investigation regarding an alleged sexual assault at the hotel where the team was staying on Sunday night.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing," Victoria Police said.

"Police spoke to a number of people at the hotel, however no-one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time."

News of the allegations yesterday sent shock waves through the league, naturally filling the slates of news bulletins and AFL panel shows.

On Channel Seven's Agenda Setters, former Port Adelaide star Kane Cornes spoke from "the football point of view" of the issue, saying the players' lack of consideration for their teammates "is what makes [him] so angry".

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney. (ABC News/ Getty Images)

"This is where I get really angry from a football point of view," he said.

"When you're two weeks away from a finals series, when Dane Rampe has played in four losing grand finals and he's probably in bed at age 36 or at home right now going, 'This is my last chance, I'm 36, I had a chance to finish second and host another home final, give myself one last chance at winning a premiership'.

"[Jake] Lloyd's played in four losing grand finals, Heeney himself has played in three. … You'd think it would mean a bit more to Isaac Heeney ... on the eve of a finals series and put your teammates and your team in jeopardy."

Loading Instagram content

On Fox Footy, Melbourne great Garry Lyon said he did not want to "understate or downplay the seriousness of" the case, insisting he could "only really comment on the one side and that is football-related matters".

"The rest will sort themselves out and again, that's not to dismiss all parties involved in this, so let's get that on the table," he said.

"What we can discuss is the ramifications from a football point of view and this is an unmitigated disaster for the Sydney Swans and for the game.

"Those pictures on the eve of the AFL finals series with plain clothes [police] and police cars outside a hotel room one week out from the finals series is an absolute disaster."

McCarthy, now a commentator for Seven and Triple M, said focusing on "the football consequences" for the team caused by any potential sanctions or distractions sent the wrong message, particularly to girls and women.

Kate McCarthy says the focus should not be on "the football consequences" of the police investigation. (Getty Images: Hancock)

The former Lion, Saint and Hawk also took issue with Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich saying the club was "extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation".

"AFL players occupy positions of enormous influence. We celebrate them as role models when they do wonderful things in the community, we can't suddenly decide they're 'just footballers' when difficult questions about behaviour, attitudes towards women and culture arise," she wrote on Instagram.

"Language matters too. Players don't simply 'find themselves in situations'. Adults have agency and make choices. Whatever this investigation ultimately determines, our language shouldn't inadvertently remove that agency or responsibility."

Current GWS player and McCarthy's former AFLW teammate, Tilly Lucas-Rodd, praised the post, while Lion star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."

Loading...

The news about the Swans emerged two weeks after former AFL player-agent Ralph Carr was revealed as the "well-connected man" convicted of rape last month.

In the wake of that revelation, former player and Australian Football Hall of Fame member Sam Newman questioned the evidence in the case and said the victim "might have buyer's remorse".

McCarthy questioned how much the AFL was doing to truly engage and include women and girls in footy spaces if someone like Newman remained in the hall of fame.

"We should be asking serious questions about what and who we continue to celebrate as a league," she wrote.

"The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates. It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise.

"This isn't about declaring anyone guilty. That is for police and the courts. When women are potentially harmed, why are we so quick to focus on what it means for the men on the football field?"

Tech.content:

Robin Williams’ children are taking over their father’s Instagram account after his daughter spoke out against the use of his AI likeness, as reported earlier by The Wrap. In a post on Tuesday, Zak, Zelda, and Cody Williams write that they want the late actor’s Instagram profile to be a “safe, trusted place where the stories, photos, videos, and memories shared reflect his legacy with authenticity, warmth, and care.”

A story posted to Zelda Williams’ own Instagram account expands on the decision to bring back her father’s profile, saying that it’s meant to help combat “rampant AI abuse,” according to The Wrap:

I’m sorry if anyone found Dad’s old page posting again to be triggering. Believe me, I know it’s a little strange. Making that space into one where people can find authentic clips and photos of him is one of the best ways we’ve now found to fight back against rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness on here.

Robin Williams’ Instagram account remained inactive following his death in 2014. Last year, Zelda Williams asked fans to stop sending her AI-generated videos of her father. “To watch the legacies of real people be condensed down to ‘this vaguely looks and sounds like them so that’s enough’, just so other people can churn out horrible TikTok slop puppeteering them is maddening,” she wrote at the time.

Though some AI chatbots have restrictions in place to prevent users from generating images or videos with the AI likeness of a public figure or celebrity, these guardrails can still be bypassed. OpenAI’s now-shuttered Sora app became a hotbed for generating videos of copyrighted characters and celebrities, while Grok is still generating sexualized AI deepfakes of famous women, according to Wired.

Zelda, Zak, and Cody Williams add that they’re going to use their father’s Instagram account to share his “unique talent and humor with the world.”

Tech.title: OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is announcing security updates following the July news that its AI broke out of a sandboxed environment and accidentally hacked Hugging Face, including improvements to its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques. The company had already put the brakes on a new model, Astra, that it thinks could have “critical” cybersecurity capabilities, and the company says it instituted a two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on its “latest models intended for deployment” while it tightened up security. The company’s “largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold.”

For its frontier model research, OpenAI now requires stronger sandboxes for workloads that “execute model-generated or otherwise untrusted code,” and has more controls to “isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet.” It has also updated its research environment to “remove potentially vulnerable shared services, reduce standing privileges, and improve security and trust boundaries.”

As part of the company’s expanded monitoring setup, OpenAI now aims to issue an alert “within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced,” OpenAI says. If the people paged after an alert can’t “conclusively” determine whether an alert is a false positive within 30 minutes, “those teams are expected to pause the activity.”

OpenAI also says that it’s applying “our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process,” including reward models that “better detect and discourage unsafe behavior” and training models “to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations.”

Since the discovery of the Hugging Face breach, Anthropic and Meta have also found that their AI models had hacked other organizations.
